title: The Archive's Empty Line
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The signature had been scraped away so thoroughly that the paper looked furry.

I leaned toward the glass, then caught myself.

"Don't breathe on it," Severus said from behind me.

"I wasn't going to."

"You were certainly preparing to."

I stepped back from the burned ledger. The page lay in its padded support beneath a reading lamp, its damaged corner resting on a strip of pale paper. Moonroot Archive smelled of linen, cool plaster, and the sharp tea Severus had refused to let me improve with more sugar.

Neri stood across the table with their hands clasped.

"The committee wants a name for the public report," they said.

"The committee wants a certainty it doesn't possess," Severus answered.

"People are angry."

"They have reason to be."

"They think we're hiding something."

I looked at Neri. "Are you?"

The question stayed in the room.

Neri didn't answer immediately. They had lived with the Closed Bells history longer than I had known this valley. I could see them choosing which memories they would allow into daylight.

"I remember a keeper who believed closing the paths was an act of protection," they said. "I remember hearing an argument. I don't remember which hand signed this page."

"Then we put that in the report," I said.

Severus nodded once. High praise.

Neri looked miserable. "It feels insufficient."

"It is insufficient," I said. "People lost their freedom to leave. We don't get to fix that by inventing a culprit."

Outside the archive window, the stone arches caught the afternoon sun. Travelers crossed the square carrying baskets and rolled maps, sometimes stopping at the notice board to read the departure rules. The freedom to come and go had become so ordinary that it was hard to remember a time when someone had needed permission.

That ordinariness was worth protecting.

Orin arrived with a folder of copied invoices. They had been studying the work orders that survived the fire and were, to Severus's delight and everyone else's exhaustion, developing a terrible habit of questioning every adjective.

"There's a difference between the date the material was ordered and the date it was delivered," Orin said, opening the folder. "Some of the reports treat them as the same day."

Severus reached for the first invoice. "A dangerous shortcut."

Orin beamed.

The evidence was precise but incomplete. Iron fittings had been ordered before the worst flood reached the valley. The bakery had fed an additional work crew. Fen's copied tide chart showed the lower channel could still have carried water on the day the closure was ordered. But we couldn't tell who signed the order or whether a later instruction had changed its meaning.

"We need to hear the people affected," I said.

Neri's expression tightened. "Some will not want to speak."

"Then we ask whether they're willing. Privately. We don't make public testimony the price of being believed."

Severus looked at me.

"That is an important distinction."

The committee meeting was less graceful.

A councilor named Avel stood and demanded to know whether the erased name could be recovered with magic. Severus explained, in a voice thin with patience, that experimental methods risked damaging the original. Another resident suggested using the name of the person who had been keeper at the time, regardless of evidence.

Neri looked as though they might agree just to end the argument.

I stood.

"Would we accept that if it were our name?" I asked.

Avel frowned. "That isn't the same."

"Why not?"

"People suffered."

"Yes. Their suffering deserves an accurate record. It doesn't become less real because the signature is blank."

A woman at the back rose slowly. "My grandfather was prevented from leaving. I don't need you to guess who held the pen. I need you to admit the system allowed it."

The room went quiet.

I didn't know her name. I didn't write it down.

Neri stood. Their hands shook.

"The doors were restricted," they said. "People who wanted to leave were turned away. We have evidence of that. It was wrong."

There was no applause. Some residents looked angry that the statement had taken so long; others looked relieved. Both responses belonged in the room.

The committee approved an updated report with the empty line preserved, the evidence categories clearly marked, and a voluntary invitation for private testimony. It also funded a review of the present emergency-exit rules, because remembering past harm without changing current procedures would have been a particularly cruel form of nostalgia.

Before the councilors left, Avel came back to the table, holding the copy of the report as if it might stain his hands.

"My grandmother was locked out when the bells stopped," he said. "If you won't put a name in that space, what are we supposed to tell her?"

Neri folded their copy carefully. "Tell her what the witnesses have said. Tell her what we know happened. Don't tell her we know who signed an order when we don't."

Avel shook his head. "That sounds like hiding."

It did, a little, if I thought about how long families had waited. I was not immune to wanting a single person whose name could carry everybody's anger.

"Can we separate the facts from the unanswered question on the public notice?" I asked. "A blank box with no explanation looks like somebody forgot to finish their work."

Orin, the archive clerk, brought out a draft layout. They'd divided the evidence into three sections: recorded closures, witness accounts and documents that needed further review. At the bottom was the scraped signature with the words *identity not established*. Avel pointed to the section where his grandmother's testimony could go.

"She doesn't want her name out there."

"She shouldn't have to put it out there," Neri said.

We worked out a way for him to carry a blank witness form home. His grandmother could speak, write, decline, or ask a trusted clerk to record only what she chose. There was no deadline for a public accusation and no requirement that she meet the council.

When he left, Avel was still angry.

I didn't blame him.

Severus returned to the reading shelf with a small folded note. "The original may be examined again after the conservation survey. Not before."

"Do you think they'll ever discover the name?"

"I think," he said, "that the answer matters enough not to fabricate."

The practical work felt painfully modest beside what people had lost. Still, Orin had new paper to prepare, a damaged record to protect, and an actual deadline for the council to publish the verified facts. I helped make copies, one by one, until my fingers were gray with dust.

Maui waited for me outside with bread from Mara. He hadn't asked how to get the lost name through strength or magic. He asked if I'd eaten.

"Ladies and gentlemen," Maui whispered, lifting the loaf as though it were a famous trophy, "the triumphant return of the only man who can solve an ancient mystery with lunch."

"That's not what the archive was doing."

"Exactly. Nobody there thought to bring lunch. Tragic oversight."

His little tattoo offered the bread a tiny salute. I smiled in spite of the ache behind my eyes.

Maui saw me look toward the archive door. His expression shifted. He wanted the scraped name to mean something he could fight. I could almost see the imaginary adversary taking shape in his mind: a villain, a rescue, a clear ending to the legend.

"Did you find the monster?" he asked at last.

"No."

He nodded, then sat beside me. "All right. Then tell me what you *did* find. Or don't. I make a fantastic audience, which you should know by now."

I tore the loaf in half. He accepted his portion and didn't ask what Severus had learned until I was ready to speak.

"No."

"Then at least one mystery can be solved."

I laughed, tired enough that it almost hurt. We ate on the steps without turning somebody else's old suffering into our romantic lesson.

When the meeting ended, Severus found me beside the reading shelf.

"You were very determined," he said.

"So were you."

"An unfortunate family resemblance."

I laughed.

Maui was waiting outside with a parcel from Fen. He had spent the afternoon checking the upper mooring rather than attending a meeting he had no technical role in. He asked what happened, and I told him as much as the witnesses had agreed could be public.

"Did you find the person responsible?" he asked.

"No."

"Then what did you get?"

"A report that tells the truth about what it knows."

He considered that as we walked through the square.

"I suppose that's better than a very convincing lie."

"Usually."

At home, he set the parcel aside and watched me put the minutes in my notebook.

"Are you still thinking about the blank line?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

I looked at the green pages, at the places in my own past where memory had refused to give me names.

"Because I've spent so long wanting an answer that I nearly forgot an answer has to be earned."

Maui sat beside me.

He didn't tell me everything would be all right. He didn't offer to tear open the archive walls.

He rested his hand beside mine, close enough for me to choose.

I did.

When the kitchen grew dark, we lit a lamp and left the notebook open. The empty line remained in the report, not a refusal to care, but a promise not to lie.
